extract:
Wilco emerged from Belleville, Illinois in 1994, formed in the immediate aftermath of the breakup of pioneering alt-country band Uncle Tupelo. When Jay Farrar left to form Son Volt, his Uncle Tupelo bandmate Jeff Tweedy gathered the remaining members—bassist John Stirratt, drummer Ken Coomer, and multi-instrumentalist Max Johnston—and added guitarist Jay Bennett shortly thereafter, christening the new outfit Wilco. They signed to Reprise Records, a Warner Bros. subsidiary, and slotted into the burgeoning mid-1990s alt-country scene alongside contemporaries like Whiskeytown, the Jayhawks, and Son Volt, with the magazine No Depression more or less treating them as flagship artists of the movement.

Their 1995 debut A.M. was a relatively straightforward roots-rock record, but Wilco's ambitions quickly outgrew the genre. The 1996 double album Being There expanded their palette toward Stones-y rock, power pop, and lo-fi experimentation, and 1999's Summerteeth pushed further still, layering Brian Wilson-indebted harmonies, Mellotrons, and studio textures over Tweedy's increasingly dark lyrics. During this period the band also collaborated with British folk legend Billy Bragg on Mermaid Avenue (1998) and Mermaid Avenue Vol. II (2000), setting unpublished Woody Guthrie lyrics to new music—projects that significantly raised their profile and earned a Grammy nomination.

The band's defining moment came with Yankee Hotel Foxtrot, recorded with engineer/collaborator Jim O'Rourke and famously rejected by Reprise, who dropped the band; Wilco streamed the album free online before Nonesuch, another Warner imprint, picked it up and released it in 2002. The record's fractured pop, tape-loop interludes, and songs like "I Am Trying to Break Your Heart," "Jesus, Etc.," and "Heavy Metal Drummer" earned widespread acclaim and a documentary, I Am Trying to Break Your Heart, directed by Sam Jones. Jay Bennett was dismissed during the album's making, and the band's lineup churned further before stabilizing with the arrival of guitarist Nels Cline and multi-instrumentalist Pat Sansone around 2004. A Ghost Is Born (2004), again featuring O'Rourke, won Grammys for Best Alternative Music Album and Best Recording Package.

From Sky Blue Sky (2007) onward, Wilco settled into a remarkably stable six-piece lineup—Tweedy, Stirratt, Cline, Sansone, drummer Glenn Kotche, and keyboardist Mikael Jorgensen—and a more relaxed, classic-rock-leaning sound, while still indulging experimental impulses on records like Wilco (The Album), The Whole Love, and the surprise-released Star Wars (2015). They launched their own label, dBpm Records, and since 2005 have curated the Solid Sound Festival at MASS MoCA in North Adams, Massachusetts, an event that doubles as a showcase for Tweedy's and the members' wide-ranging side projects.

Critically, Wilco have long been treated as one of America's most important rock bands of their generation, frequently compared to a latter-day version of acts like the Band or Big Star for the way they fuse traditional songcraft with restless studio experimentation. Tweedy has also pursued a productive solo and memoir-writing career, releasing the autobiography Let's Go (So We Can Get Back) in 2018. The group remains active, having released Cruel Country in 2022 and Cousin, produced by Cate Le Bon, in 2023, and continues to tour and record without any apparent intention of slowing down.
title: Wilco
